hero.title: Couples Living Together Test | Are You Ready to Move In?
hero.intro1: You already sleep at each other's place 5 nights a week. You have a toothbrush at his place, he has a drawer at yours. At this point, the question isn't "do we love each other enough to live together" but rather: can we share 600 square feet without killing each other?
hero.intro2: Because living together isn't just extending the weekends. It's discovering that the other person leaves their socks lying around. That their definition of "clean" isn't the same as yours. That silence for two isn't the same as silence alone. And that those cute little habits from the first months can become really annoying after six.

seo.s1Title: Moving in together: the real test for your relationship
seo.s1p1: Everyone tells you it's "the next step." After a few months of dating, the question comes up. "What if we got a place together?" Sounds simple. It isn't.
seo.s1p2: Living together means going from the "best version of yourself", the one you bring to a date, to the full version: the one who snores, leaves the light on and eats cereal at 11pm. It's a real-life crash test for your relationship. And contrary to what people assume, post-move-in breakups almost never come from the big issues. They come from the daily micro-frictions that pile up because nobody dares raise them.
seo.s1p3: The toothpaste tube. The bedroom temperature. The volume of the music in the morning. Ridiculous? Yes. But after 6 months, a poorly squeezed toothpaste tube can become the symbol of everything you never said.
seo.s2Title: The 6 topics nobody brings up (that ruin everything)
seo.s2r1Text: Not "we'll split things." Specifically. Who pays for what? Joint account or not? 50/50 or proportional to income? What happens if one of you loses their job? Rent is only the beginning: add the bills, the electricity, the internet, the groceries, and it climbs fast. Couples who lay out the numbers before signing the lease defuse most money arguments before they even exist: it's rarely the amount that hurts, it's the surprise.
seo.s2r2Text: More than money, more than jealousy, it is the division of chores that creates the most resentment in couples who live together. And the trap is that it settles in quietly. At first, one person does more because "it doesn't bother them." Then it becomes expected. Then a frustration. Then a reproach. Talk about it beforehand: who does what, how often, and to what standard.
seo.s2r3Text: Loving someone and needing alone time aren't contradictory. But when you share 500 square feet, "I need some space" can sound like rejection. It has to be said in advance. Plan a spot, however small, where each of you can withdraw. Accept that the other can close a door without it meaning something is wrong. Couples who know each other well handle this naturally.
seo.s2r4Text: One gets up at 6 AM to go running. The other works until midnight. These schedule gaps, when you're living together 7 days a week, become a real issue.
seo.s2r5Text: Your apartment is also the other person's home. Their best friend turning up on a Sunday unannounced, your sister staying "just one night" and leaving four days later. Home is a refuge. When that refuge is invaded without your consent, it breeds resentment. Set the rules together.
seo.s2r6Title: The "what if it doesn't work out?" question
seo.s2r6Text: Nobody wants to think about it. But it is a bit like insurance: it makes no sense to skip it on the grounds that you "probably won't need it". Who keeps the apartment if you break up? Whose name is on the lease? What happens to the furniture you bought together? Talking about this doesn't jinx anything. It protects both of you.
seo.s3Title: How long should you date before moving in together?
seo.s3p1: 6 months. 1 year. 2 years. Everyone has an opinion. The reality is that there's no magic number.
seo.s3p2: What matters is what you've experienced together, not the number of months on the clock. A couple who saw each other three times a week for two years has spent less time together than a couple who were practically under the same roof after six months. The real criterion is this: have you already been through a serious conflict? Have you seen the other one when they are not at their best, ill, stressed, exhausted, in a foul mood three days running? If the answer is no, you only know the shop-window version. And moving in with a shop-window version is setting yourself up for surprises.
seo.s3p3: A couple in love is great. A couple in love that knows what daily life together actually looks like is even better.
seo.s4Title: Moving in for the right reasons (and not the wrong ones)
seo.s4p1: The right reasons: you want to build a daily life together, you've tested it and it works, you are on the same page about the practical questions, and the wish is genuine on both sides.
seo.s4p3: "It'll be cheaper for two." Moving in together to split the rent is a roommate plan, not a couple plan.
seo.s4p4: "It's been 2 years, it's time." The social calendar has nothing to do with your emotional calendar. Some couples move in at eight months and it goes fine. Others wait four years and that is the right call. The pressure to "move forward" has destroyed more couples than it has helped.
seo.s4p5: "We'll see how it goes." Couples who know how to solve their problems are the ones who last under the same roof.
seo.s5Title: The first 3 months: what nobody tells you
seo.s5p1: The first 3 months of cohabitation are the adjustment period. Not the honeymoon you were sold. Here is what to expect, concretely.
seo.s5p2: Month 1 is the excitement. Everything is new. You decorate, you shop together, you cook for two. It's lovely.
seo.s5p3: Month 2, habits settle in. And the first frictions along with them. Why is there always washing-up in the sink? Why does she take 45 minutes in the bathroom every morning? That is normal. That is adjustment.
seo.s5p4: Month 3 is the moment of truth. The excitement has worn off, reality is here. If you get past this point by talking, even clumsily, you are on the right track. If the unsaid piles up, this is the moment to say it. Not in six months. Now.
seo.s5p5: One piece of advice long-settled couples always give: keep moments of your own even when you live together. See your friends alone, keep a hobby that is just yours, go out without the other. That is not a lack of love. It is what lets you keep things light in your relationship instead of turning it into functional cohabitation.
seo.s6Title: Practical checklist before moving in together
seo.s6p1: The concrete points to sort out before you unpack your boxes in the same place:
seo.s6p2: The budget. Make a spreadsheet, an actual one. Rent, utilities, groceries, going out, savings. Put the numbers side by side. If it is already tight before you move in, it will not sort itself out once the lease is signed.
seo.s6p3: The lease. Under whose name? Both names on the lease means both are liable for the rent. A single name means the other has no claim on the home if you separate. Worth thinking through.
seo.s6p4: The furniture. Who brings what? What do you buy together? Bear in mind that a sofa bought by two people is a potential negotiation if you break up.
seo.s6p5: The ground rules. Not a contract signed at a solicitor's. Just a verbal agreement on the things that matter: cleanliness, guests, noise, personal space. It can happen over a pizza. What matters is that it gets said.
seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions about living together

faq.q: Is it normal to feel stressed about moving in together?
faq.a: Yes. It's actually a good sign. It means you are taking the step seriously instead of charging in blind. The "will we make it work?" kind of stress is healthy. The "do I actually want this?" kind deserves a longer pause.

faq.q: Should you do a trial run before signing a lease?
faq.a: It's not mandatory, but it's smart. Spend 3-4 consecutive weeks at one person's place. Not in holiday mode, in daily-life mode: work, shopping, cleaning, Tuesday-evening tiredness. If you survive a rainy Tuesday night in November in a studio flat together, you will survive a fair bit.

faq.q: How do you handle income differences when living together?
faq.a: A strict 50/50 split isn't the only option. Many couples opt for a proportional split based on income. Others prefer a shared pot for the fixed costs, with each keeping whatever is left. There is no universal formula. The only mistake is not discussing it.

faq.q: Will moving in together kill the passion?
faq.a: Not if you're intentional about it. What kills passion is not living together in itself, it is a routine nobody tends to. Couples who keep their rituals, a weekly date night, small surprises, moments of intimate connection, those are the ones who thrive.

faq.q: What if one person is ready and the other isn't?
faq.a: Don't force it. Moving in together is a two-person decision or it's no decision at all. If one of you is hesitating, find out why. Is it fear? A practical problem? Or a doubt about the relationship itself? If you're struggling to communicate about it, that may be exactly where certain patterns in your relationship are surfacing.

faq.q: Is it better to rent a new place together or move into one person's apartment?
faq.a: Ideally, a fresh space for both of you. Moving into "the other person's place" creates an imbalance: one of you is home, the other is a permanent guest. If the budget rules out a move, at the very least redo the place together so both of you feel at home in it.
